title-group.article-title: Effect of dyspnoea-oriented hypnosis as an adjunct to pulmonary rehabilitation on the affective dimension of dyspnoea and physical activity level: a randomised controlled trial

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Pulmonary rehabilitation has limited long-term effects on physical activity levels in patients with COPD. Dyspnoea-related anxiety, part of the affective dimension of dyspnoea, is a major barrier to physical activity. This study assessed whether hypnosis as an adjunct to standard pulmonary rehabilitation could improve the affective dimension of dyspnoea, as well as physical activity levels, 6 months after rehabilitation.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In a randomised, open-label trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04010825), 106 COPD patients were enrolled to receive either conventional 4-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (CONT) or pulmonary rehabilitation plus five 1-h hypnosis sessions (HYPNO) primarily targeting emotional dyspnoea management. The primary outcome was the evolution of the affective dimension of dyspnoea at 6 months, assessed by the Multidimensional Dyspnoea Profile questionnaire. Secondary outcomes included changes in physical activity levels via the Simple Physical Activity Questionnaire.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Affective dyspnoea scores decreased after pulmonary rehabilitation in both groups (p<0.01). At 6 months, improvement persisted only in the HYPNO group (p<0.001 versus baseline), whereas the CONT group returned to baseline (p=0.98). Physical activity levels increased only in the HYPNO group (p<0.05 versus baseline) and were higher than in the CONT group at follow-up (p<0.001). Changes in physical activity levels correlated with changes in affective dyspnoea (r= −0.26, p<0.05).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The results suggest that a brief intervention of five hypnosis sessions, as an adjunct to pulmonary rehabilitation, maintained the benefits of pulmonary rehabilitation on the affective dimension of dyspnoea 6 months after pulmonary rehabilitation. The improvement in the affective dimension of dyspnoea was associated with an increase in physical activity levels, a key goal of pulmonary rehabilitation that is poorly achieved in usual pulmonary rehabilitation programmes.

p.bold: A five-session hypnosis intervention as an adjunct to pulmonary rehabilitation helps maintain emotional relief from dyspnoea and increases physical activity levels for ≥6 months, addressing important goals often not met by standard programmes

sec.p: Received 2025 May 7; Accepted 2025 Aug 1; Collection date 2026 Jan.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pulmonary rehabilitation is one of the most effective treatments for COPD. Its two main objectives are “to improve the physical and psychological condition of people with chronic respiratory disease and to promote the long-term adherence of health-enhancing behaviours” [1], but unfortunately, in its conventional form, it fails to achieve the second objective. Indeed, it has been reported to be poorly effective in inducing changes in physical activity levels after a pulmonary rehabilitation stay, with low effect sizes and with conflicting results [2]. This may explain the well-documented loss of health benefits in the months following pulmonary rehabilitation [3–5]. Optimising the effects of pulmonary rehabilitation on physical activity levels thus remains an important issue.

Among the various barriers to physical activity in COPD, dyspnoea-related anxiety (or dyspnoea-related fear), a component of the affective dimension of dyspnoea [6], is one of the most important [7–10]. This is explained by the fact that in many patients, the anticipation of dyspnoea during exercise leads to activity avoidance mechanisms [9, 11]. A recent study by our team showed that 70% of patients improved their affective dyspnoea score after pulmonary rehabilitation [12], indicating the treatability of this dimension. The use of complementary treatments during pulmonary rehabilitation to strengthen the effects on the affective dimension of dyspnoea and, most importantly, with sustained effects over time, is therefore a promising way for increasing and maintaining sufficient physical activity in the long term.

To achieve this goal, the use of hypnosis as an adjunct to pulmonary rehabilitation could be a treatment of choice. Its immediate efficacy in alleviating experimentally induced dyspnoea in healthy subjects has already been demonstrated [13]. In addition, in COPD patients, a single hypnosis session reduced anxiety and respiratory rate [14]. Another study demonstrated an improvement in exercise tolerance after three sessions of hypnosis in addition to pulmonary rehabilitation, which was possibly linked to an improvement in dyspnoea tolerance [15]. Furthermore, the use of hypnosis to enhance the effects of pulmonary rehabilitation seems particularly promising. First, results are seen quite quickly, with significant effects after one to three sessions, whereas usual psychological intervention techniques, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, sometimes require up to 10 sessions [15]. Second, teaching self-hypnosis as a supplement could provide a lasting tool that patients can use on their own, away from the pulmonary rehabilitation stage, to limit the activity avoidance mechanism associated with an overly pronounced emotional aspect of breathing difficulties at home.

Our aim was therefore to evaluate the effect of a hypnosis intervention that primarily targets dyspnoea-related anxiety and the affective component of dyspnoea, on the affective dimension of dyspnoea after pulmonary rehabilitation. We hypothesised that hypnosis as an adjunct to pulmonary rehabilitation would lead to greater improvement in the affective dimension of dyspnoea at 6 months. A second aim was to assess the effects on physical activity level.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The present study was a single-centre, open-label, randomised controlled trial with a 1:1 ratio. After giving consent, participants were randomised to receive pulmonary rehabilitation plus a personalised hypnotic intervention (treatment group (HYPNO)) or pulmonary rehabilitation alone (control group (CONT)). The protocol was approved by an independent French Ethics Committee (CPP Ouest III; reference number: 2019-A00874-53). The protocol and statistical analysis plan were pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04010825).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Participants were adults scheduled for a 4-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation programme at the Clinique du Souffle La Vallonie (Lodève, France) between October 2019 and June 2023 (with an 8-month recruitment pause between March and October 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic). Inclusion criteria were a diagnosis of COPD confirmed by a forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio <0.70 after bronchodilator intake, a predicted FEV1 <80%, age 40–75 years and a health insurance. Exclusion criteria were inability to answer a questionnaire, a delusional mental disorder, pregnant women or participation in another study, except observational studies. These criteria were checked during the inclusion visit which took place during the first 2 days of pulmonary rehabilitation. No incentive was provided to encourage participation in the study.

sec.title: Randomisation
sec.p: The randomisation sequence was computer generated by the methodologist and concealed until formal patient enrolment, after consent to participate and completion of baseline assessment.

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: All patients underwent a multidisciplinary and individualised inpatient rehabilitation according to the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society statement [1]. The 4-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation programme has been described elsewhere [16]. Briefly, it consisted of endurance, resistance and balance training, relaxation therapy, breathing exercises, and group and individual education sessions focusing on symptoms management, nutrition counselling, psychological support and smoking cessation support.

sec.title: Hypnotic intervention
sec.p: Patients in the HYPNO group received five 60-min individual hypnosis sessions aimed at reducing personal barriers to physical activity, with a focus on dyspnoea-related anxiety and emotional dyspnoea management. The intervention was delivered face-to-face by a clinical health psychologist with certified advanced training in clinical hypnosis. Scripts for each hypnosis sessions were developed in collaboration with a team of experts from the Institut Milton H. Erickson Toulouse Occitanie, Toulouse, France (IMHETO; www.imheto.com). To engage the patients in hypnosis, at the beginning of the first session, the therapist explained the principles of hypnosis and dispelled misconceptions and doubts. The sessions consisted of the following four stages: 1) hypnotic induction, through suggestions made to promote a state of relaxation and focused awareness; 2) deepening procedure, in which a more deeply relaxed and focused state was achieved through further suggestions; 3) symptom-specific therapeutic suggestions, through the therapeutic use of dissociation with specific suggestions aimed at changing or improving symptoms or behaviours; and 4) reorientation–awakening stage, in which the patient returns to the here and now, accompanied by positive post-hypnotic suggestions and training for the use of self-hypnosis. At the end of the last session the therapist provided a written guide on how to practise self-hypnosis at home. Full details of the comprehensive hypnosis script and the self-hypnosis guide can be found in the supplementary material.

sec.title: Measures
sec.p: In addition to the standard comprehensive assessment of the programme (clinical evaluation, body composition, respiratory function and cardiopulmonary exercise testing), the patients were assessed three times: at baseline (T1), after pulmonary rehabilitation (T2) and 6 months after pulmonary rehabilitation (T3).

sec.title: Clinical characteristics
sec.p: Data from the standard comprehensive assessment of the programme including sex, age, body mass index (BMI), comorbidities, respiratory function and exercise capacity (distance on the 6-min walk test (6MWT)) were collected at baseline in the patient medical records. In addition, 6MWT distance was also collected at T2.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: The primary outcome was the change in the affective dimension of dyspnoea from T1 to T3 as measured by the Multidimensional Dyspnoea Profile (MDP) questionnaire [6, 17]. The MDP questionnaire includes 11 items. Patients were asked to answer the questions by focusing on the worst dyspnoea experience that occurred in the last week [18]. The affective dimension was calculated as the sum of the scores for the immediate breathing discomfort question and the intensity of the five emotional response questions [18].

sec.title: Secondary outcomes
sec.p: The sensory dimension of dyspnoea was assessed as the sum of the five sensory quality items of the MDP questionnaire [18], as described for the primary outcome.

The impact dimension of dyspnoea was assessed using the London Chest of Activity Daily Living (LCADL) questionnaire [19, 20]. The LCADL was developed to assess dyspnoea related to activities of daily living in patients with COPD. It consists of a total of 15 items in four domains: personal care (four items), household (six items), physical (two items) and leisure (three items).

Physical activity and sedentary time were assessed using the Simple Physical Activity Questionnaire (SIMPAQ) [21]. SIMPAQ consists of five questions asking for time spent in bed overnight (item 1), sedentary time including naps (item 2), time spent walking (item 3), time spent in structured physical activity (item 4) and time spent in leisure time (item 5), averaged over the last 7 days. Time spent walking (item 3) and time spent exercising (item 4) were combined to provide an estimate of total self-reported moderate–vigorous physical activity (MVPA) time [22].
Post-traumatic stress disorder was assessed using the Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist Scale (PCLS), in 17 items [23].

Anxiety and depression scores were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) [24]. HADS is a 14-item scale consisting of an anxiety subscale (HADS-A) and a depression subscale (HADS-D).
Health-related quality of life was assessed using the COPD Assessment Test (CAT) questionnaire, in eight items [25].
The number of exacerbations and hospitalisations in the past 6 months was self-reported and assessed only at T1 and T3.
A self-report questionnaire was designed to assess the weekly frequency of self-hypnosis use in the past 6 months, as well as any other relaxation or hypnosis session experience.

sec.title: Sample size
sec.p: The sample size was thus based on a mean±sd difference between groups of −3.9±5.8 in the primary outcome (affective dimension of dyspnoea as measured by the MDP) at T3, derived from the available literature [18, 26]. The study was powered at 90% with a two-sided α risk set at 0.05 and required 29 participants per group. The sample size was inflated by 25% to account for attrition to give a final target of 38 participants per group, 76 in total. At the time of protocol design (2018), no published data were available regarding the effect of hypnosis on dyspnoea in COPD patients. The sample size calculation was therefore based on the expected mean difference and variability from non-hypnosis interventions targeting dyspnoea. It was assumed that adding a hypnosis intervention would not substantially alter the variance of the primary outcome. An interim analysis conducted mid-recruitment allowed us to reassess this assumption and adjust the required sample size accordingly. This interim analysis was carried out with the approval of the Ethics Committee at mid-recruitment to check power, after which the number of subjects required was increased to 53 per group, 106 in total. It is important to note that the initial sample size calculation was based on a between-group comparison of the change in the primary outcome (T3–T1) using the t-test. However, this was not the most suitable approach given the study design. The final analysis used a more appropriate linear mixed model to account for within-subject correlations and the repeated measures design.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Independent sample t-tests and Chi-squared tests were used to compare baseline group characteristics.

To examine the effect of the intervention on the outcomes, two-way mixed ANOVA was performed examining the effects of time (T1 versus T2 versus T3), group (HYPNO versus CONT) and their interaction. The underlying assumptions of ANOVA were checked using skewness–kurtosis coefficients (normality of distribution) and the Mauchly test (sphericity of variance). When the analyses revealed a significant interaction or main effect, a Tukey post-hoc test was used for pairwise comparisons.
The association between the changes in the affective dimension score of dyspnoea and physical activity levels between T1 and T3 was assessed using Spearman's test.

Subgroup analyses examined the influence of self-hypnosis on all outcomes (i.e. dyspnoea, activity, psychological and burden data) by comparing patients in the HYPNO group who used self-hypnosis with those who did not using ANOVA.
Data are presented as mean with standard deviation in the case of normal distribution (Shapiro–Wilk test) or otherwise as median with interquartile range (IQR).
All statistical analyses were performed using JASP version 0.19.3 (https://jasp-stats.org). Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 for all analyses.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: 106 patients were randomised in the study. One patient no longer met the criteria after the baseline assessment, 13 patients (six and seven in the HYPNO and CONT groups, respectively) did not complete pulmonary rehabilitation and 15 patients (six and nine in the HYPNO and CONT groups, respectively) were lost to follow-up at T3. The final sample consisted of 40 and 37 patients in the HYPNO and CONT groups, respectively (figure 1). There were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between groups (table 1).

sec.title: Affective dimension of dyspnoea (primary outcome)
sec.p: Contrary to our hypothesis, there were no significant differences at T3 between the HYPNO and CONT groups (p=0.18) (figure 2a). The score of the affective dimension of dyspnoea decreased significantly after pulmonary rehabilitation in both groups (p<0.01 and p<0.001 in the CONT and HYPNO groups, respectively). However, only the HYPNO group remained improved 6 months after pulmonary rehabilitation (p<0.001 compared to baseline), whereas the CONT group worsened (no difference from T1 with p=0.98 and increase from T2 with p<0.05). In addition, the evolution between T3 and T1 in the HYPNO group was significantly better than in the CONT group (−12.3±17 versus −1.75±15; t=2.8, p=0.006) (figure 2b).

sec.title: Sensory and impact dimensions of dyspnoea (secondary outcomes)
sec.p: In the HYPNO group, the score of the sensory dimension of dyspnoea was lower at T2 (p<0.001) and T3 (p<0.01) compared to T1. Conversely, there were no significant changes in the CONT group. In addition, the sensory dimension score was higher in the CONT group compared to the HYPNO group at T3 (p<0.01).

The LCADL impact dimension score decreased significantly after pulmonary rehabilitation in both groups (p<0.001). However, the benefits were not maintained 6 months after rehabilitation (p>0.05 compared to baseline).

sec.title: Physical activity and sedentary time (secondary outcomes)
sec.p: MVPA increased only in the HYPNO group compared to T1 (p<0.05) (figure 3). In addition, MVPA was higher in the HYPNO group compared to the CONT group at T3 (p<0.001). As for MVPA, the sedentary time was only reduced in the HYPNO group (p<0.05).

sec.title: Other secondary outcomes
sec.p: We found a comparable pattern of improvement between the HYPNO and CONT groups in their quality of life (CAT) and depression (HADS-D) scores, with a significant decrease immediately after pulmonary rehabilitation, but with no further benefit at 6 months (no difference from baseline).

Regarding the scores for anxiety (HADS-A) and post-traumatic symptoms (PCLS), there was a significant improvement immediately after rehabilitation in both groups, but the improvement was maintained 6 months after pulmonary rehabilitation only in the HYPNO group (all p<0.001 compared to baseline).
There were no significant changes in the number of exacerbations or hospitalisations in the 6 months before and after rehabilitation in either group (all p>0.05).

sec.title: Association between the evolution of the affective dimension of dyspnoea and of the level of physical activity
sec.p: The correlation analysis revealed an inverse relationship between the evolution of the affective dimension of dyspnoea (T3–T1) and the evolution of MVPA (r= −0.26, p<0.05).

sec.title: Impact of self-hypnosis practice on outcomes
sec.p: Of the 40 patients in the treatment group, 26 reported using self-hypnosis at home in the 6 months following rehabilitation (65%), while 13 reported never using it. For one patient the information could not be retrieved. We found no differences between the patients with or without self-hypnosis used in all outcomes (i.e. dyspnoea, activity, psychological and burden data), but with limited power due to limited sample size to perform mixed ANOVAs.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This randomised controlled study aimed to assess the effects of a hypnosis intervention as an adjunct to a standard inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation programme on the affective dimension of dyspnoea and on physical activity levels 6 months after the programme. Our results show that both the control (CONT) and treatment (HYPNO) groups had a significant improvement (decrease) in the affective dimension score of dyspnoea after rehabilitation, but only the HYPNO group maintained the improvement 6 months later. In addition, physical activity levels (MVPA) increased only in the HYPNO group 6 months after rehabilitation. In other secondary outcomes, the HYPNO group showed better benefits than the CONT group at 6 months, such as on the sensory dimension score of dyspnoea, sedentary time, anxiety levels (HADS-A score) and post-traumatic symptoms (PCLS score).

The HYPNO and CONT groups showed improvements in the affective dimension of dyspnoea immediately after pulmonary rehabilitation, thereby confirming the findings of previous studies [10]. However, a 6-month follow-up investigation revealed that the improvement was only sustained in the HYPNO group. The prolonged effects on this variable only obtained in the HYPNO group are consistent with the documented long-term effects of hypnosis on anxiety [27]. Although our main hypothesis was not confirmed, since there was no significant difference between the two groups on this variable at T3, the overall results underline the failure of usual pulmonary rehabilitation programmes to improve the affective dimension of dyspnoea in the medium term and demonstrate the potential of hypnosis to extend the benefits.

In line with these results, we also found better benefits 6 months after rehabilitation in the HYPNO group on other closely related outcomes such as the sensory dimension score of dyspnoea, anxiety levels and post-traumatic symptoms. It is well established that the benefits of pulmonary rehabilitation fade over time [3–5]. In our study, only patients in the CONT group showed a drop in benefits close to that reported in the literature. Therefore, and although the maintenance of benefits by hypnosis was not found for all outcomes (quality of life, dyspnoea impact dimension and depression score), our study highlights the potential of hypnosis as a complement to pulmonary rehabilitation to promote long-term improvement in health outcomes in COPD patients.

A secondary hypothesis was that addressing dyspnoea-related anxiety would have an impact on physical activity levels after rehabilitation. We observed an increase in physical activity only in the HYPNO group. Dyspnoea-related anxiety (or dyspnoea-related fear), a component of the affective dimension of dyspnoea, is one of the most important barriers to physical activity in COPD [7–9]. The correlation between improving the affective dimension of dyspnoea and improving physical activity is consistent with this claim. However, it is not possible to establish a causal relationship from our study or, if so, the direction of the relationship between improved symptoms and improved physical activity. Furthermore, although the hypnosis intervention preferentially targeted dyspnoea-related anxiety, it cannot be ruled out that some hypnotic suggestions may have had a direct effect on the patients’ physical activity. Beyond these considerations, our results provide important clinical insights. For example, a growing strategy for increasing physical activity levels in the long term is to set up a pulmonary rehabilitation maintenance programme lasting several months, which can be particularly costly and time-consuming [28]. This study shows that by simply adding a 5-h hypnosis intervention to pulmonary rehabilitation, it is possible to achieve medium-term effects on physical activity levels, with an interesting potential for efficiency.

Our intervention did not significantly reduce the number of exacerbations or hospitalisations in the 6 months after rehabilitation. The level of physical activity, which was improved by our intervention at 6 months, is an important determinant of disease burden in COPD [29]. In our study, it is possible that the follow-up period of only 6 months was insufficient to observe such effects and that patients in the CONT group continued to benefit from the protective effects of the rehabilitation programme on these outcomes [30]. It would therefore be interesting to determine whether hypnosis could lead to a reduction in disease burden over a longer follow-up period.

We found no effect of self-hypnosis practice on any of the study outcomes. We suggested that teaching and subsequent use of self-hypnosis by patients, alone, in the home, might contribute to the long-term maintenance of pulmonary rehabilitation benefits. Although self-hypnosis was an integral part of the proposed hypnosis intervention, our study was not designed to explore its effects. Consequently, our study does not allow us to know whether the teaching and practice of self-hypnosis may have played a role or whether the five hypnosis sessions alone would have been sufficient.

Despite its contributions, our study has several limitations that may limit the generalisability of the results. It was a single-centre study, conducted in an inpatient rehabilitation setting, with a single hypnosis provider. In addition, there was no sham hypnosis intervention in the CONT group, so a potential placebo effect on some outcomes cannot be ruled out. It should be acknowledged that the fact that patients in the HYPNO group received extra care could have had an impact on the results. Adding sham hypnosis sessions for the CONT group would have allowed to control for this effect. Importantly, although this adds some mechanistic uncertainty to the effects of hypnosis, it does not call into question the clinical effectiveness of our intervention. It is also important to note that a substantial number of patients dropped out or were lost to follow-up, with 12 in the HYPNO group and 16 in the CONT group not being assessed at T2 or T3. This attrition could potentially lead to an overestimation of the overall effects of pulmonary rehabilitation in both groups, as data may be disproportionately missing for participants who did not benefit from the intervention or who experienced worse outcomes. However, both the number and the reasons for dropout were comparable between groups, suggesting that attrition was unlikely to have introduced systematic bias favouring one group over the other. As a result, while the overall magnitude of the observed effects of pulmonary rehabilitation might be inflated, the internal validity of the comparison remains preserved and the estimate of the additional effect attributable to the intervention under study (hypnosis) is unlikely to be biased. Another point is that the initial power calculation did not fully account for the complexity of the mixed model analysis used in the final statistical approach. The final analysis used a more appropriate linear mixed model to account for within-subject correlations and the repeated measures design. The power of the interaction on the main outcome was within an acceptable range (0.78), meaning that adopting this statistical approach does not compromise the power of the study. Additionally, the absence of a significant between-group difference at 6 months may reflect the overly narrow formulation of our primary hypothesis, which did not account for longitudinal trends. A more appropriate hypothesis would have focused on group differences in the evolution of the affective dimension of dyspnoea over time. The significant group-by-time interaction suggests that the intervention had a meaningful and sustained effect over time, an effect that cannot be captured by a simple comparison at the final time-point. Another limitation is that physical activity levels, although based on a validated method [21, 22], were self-reported estimates rather than direct observations. Finally, physical activity could only be assessed twice (before and 6 months after rehabilitation). The questionnaire used asked about activity during the previous 7 days. This made it difficult to measure physical activity immediately after rehabilitation, as the level of physical activity during the last 7 days of the rehabilitation stay was directly dependent on the amount of activity in the programme itself and could not reflect spontaneous activity.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our study shows that a brief intervention consisting of five sessions of hypnosis focused primarily on dyspnoea emotional management, as an adjunct to pulmonary rehabilitation, can maintain the pulmonary rehabilitation benefits on the affective dimension of dyspnoea for at least 6 months. Improvement in the affective dimension of dyspnoea was also associated with an increase in physical activity levels 6 months after the programme, a key goal of pulmonary rehabilitation that is poorly achieved with usual pulmonary rehabilitation programmes.
